card: Hegel travelled on past towns, many sea-going ships and wide green meadows, in good weather, and arrived in The Hague after 8 in the evening. This was the farthest point of his journey, from which he would turn back, but first he planned to see the North Sea the next day.

Hegel was lodging in Brussels with Mr. van Ghert, at whose house he had spent the night. On arriving the previous evening he had gone straight to the letter post, but the office was already closed. His only news from Marie so far was the letter he received in Cassel; he would learn within the hour whether more had come.

card: Hegel travelled from Amsterdam via Utrecht and Deventer, then by post wagon with a gentleman from Hildesheim, Mr. Cludius, reaching Osnabrück at 5 am on Wednesday; there he visited Prof. Abeken and saw the hall of the Peace of Westphalia. He reached Bremen Thursday at nightfall and Hamburg by express post on 18 October, seeing fireworks there that evening.

Hegel was in Coblenz, writing at a window overlooking the Rhine, the bridge and Ehrenbreitstein, while eating grapes. He had been to the post office early that morning and found no letter from Marie. It was Immanuel's birthday, and he intended to drink an extra glass to him at midday.

Hegel and Mr. van Ghert walked the Waterloo battlefield for 3–4 hours on Friday and on Saturday saw the Brussels gallery, St. Gudula church and Laeken palace. On Sunday afternoon they went to Ghent, attended the university's rectorate handover there on Monday until 1 o'clock, then left by cabriolet at 2:30, reaching the Scheldt bank opposite Antwerp after 10 pm.

In Coblenz, Hegel had been shown rooms that were bomb-proof and dry, with the explanations given in local dialect, and had to change into his third shirt of the day. It rained without stopping that afternoon, so he slept. He was going to a meal, meant to visit Government Councillor Lange that evening, and planned Bonn next, then Cologne.

Hegel and his companion had spent a night at Flamandsch Hooft (Point of Flanders). Their road was paved like the Königsstraße in Berlin, tree-lined, and ran between fields, gardens and meadows; unlike around Aachen and Liège they met no beggars, village children wore shoes, many of them wooden, and stockings, and they passed through a village of 15,000 inhabitants.

The previous morning Hegel and his companion had crossed the Scheldt into Antwerp, a city of 60,000 to 70,000 inhabitants, as is Ghent. He visited the cathedral, whose nave has 3 rows of columns on each side and no pews or benches; each visitor takes one of a stack of 100 chairs and carries it from altar to altar.

Hegel obtained his ticket for the express coach. The day before, he had been told that all seats for Tuesday and Friday were taken, though passengers could still apply for extra coaches. When he enquired that day, three people from Prague applied at the same time, but for Wednesday rather than Tuesday, so he took a seat for Wednesday.

Hegel visited Schönbrunn again in the afternoon, including the menagerie grounds, where he saw only the elephant and the ostrich because the others had already retired for the night. It was too dark to see the plants. In the evening, with no Fodor, Dardanelli or Lablache performing, he saw part of a Leopoldstadt theatre piece and brought away the playbill.

Hegel left Prague after 11 o'clock and travelled in sunshine through the Bohemian countryside and its villages. By evening there was a full moon. He expected to reach Töplitz at noon the next day and Dresden the following evening, or perhaps only on Sunday.
checked: mended: place "On the road from Prague to Töplitz (stopping place not named)" was not a town name and the card names no town for the evening, so place set to Prague, the last town on his route (Töplitz and Dresden are only expected); card text unchanged

card: On Sunday Hegel drank at the Töplitz spring, walked in the Clary park, bathed and went up the Schlackenberg again, then left by carriage at 11. He crossed a range of hills in about 1½ hours, with a view to Lowositz, then crossed the Eger twice, the second time by moonlight, towards Meldros. On Monday he reached Prague at 11.

card: In the morning Hegel visited the picture gallery and the art exhibition and went up onto the Brühl Terrace, where he had also been the day before. He had also spent an hour with Ammon. After finishing his letter he was going back to the gallery and then to Tieck.

Hegel reached Vienna after 6 the previous evening, travelling 42 miles from Prague in 36 hours by express coach with a couple returning from Karlsbad and Archduke Charles's physician. He took a room at the Erzherzog Karl, went to the Italian opera, a Mercadante piece with Rubini, Donzelli, Lablache and Eckerlin, and then found Lilli and Klein at the inn.

Hegel passed through Herzberg at midday on Monday, where a country preacher's niece joined him as far as Dresden. On arrival he found Privy Councillor Schulze at his inn and persuaded him to delay his departure by a day. That morning the two visited Böttiger, the picture gallery and Böttiger's lecture, where they went through the antiquities again.

Hegel spent the whole day on his feet in the Esterhazy gallery and at Schönbrunn, where he ate, and was due at the Italian opera half an hour after writing. The weather had cleared the previous afternoon, and the day was fine and not too hot.

The previous day Hegel saw Romeo and Juliet performed by the English company in Paris, with Kemble as Romeo. In this staging Juliet wakes in the last act while Romeo, who has already taken the poison, is still alive. In the first-meeting scene Romeo sits beside Juliet before speaking, and Mercutio jokes with the Nurse when she interrupts them.

The previous day Hegel visited Versailles and the Grand and Petit Trianon. The Trianons are furnished; the palace is not. The garden has 130 marble statues, and the oldest tree in the orangery was planted in 1420. The Trianon grounds are in the English style, with artificial rocks and Swiss cottages. He did not see the fountains play.

Two days earlier, after a first night in a supplementary coach with four passengers, Hegel reached Halle at midday, fetched Hinrichs, ate and slept in the afternoon; at 6 p.m. he left for Nordhausen with one student and slept most of the night. The previous day, from 6 a.m., he travelled with students from Nordhausen to Kassel.

Hegel walked in the park along the Ilm. At 2 p.m. he dined at Goethe's, seated beside him, with Fräulein von Pogwisch, Hofrat Vogel, Dr. Emmerich (Goethe's secretary), the two grandsons, Goethe's son and Zelter; Frau von Goethe, expecting her confinement, was absent. Hegel told Goethe about politics and literature in France. That evening he went to the theatre.

Hegel arrived in Luxembourg by diligence; Herr von Hanfstengel took him on a walk through the town and part of the fortifications. He booked the diligence to Metz for the next morning. A fellow passenger from Löwen, returning from a Rhine tour after losing a son of 21 and a daughter of 17, invited Hegel to visit him there.

At 10 o'clock the previous evening, while Hegel was waiting for soup in his room in Kassel, Heinrich Beer and his wife walked in; the meeting was unplanned. Beer was returning directly from Kassel and could tell Marie that he had found Hegel well.

When Hegel got off the express coach in Kassel the previous evening, a young man was already waiting for him on behalf of his father, Conrector Matthias, the father of one of Hegel's students, to invite him to stay at their house. Hegel declined.

The previous day Hegel and Cousin went from Cologne to Bonn, visiting Windischmann and then, together, Herr von Schlegel. That morning they saw Cologne Cathedral again, the Wallraff collection and the Dying Mary, and ate oysters with Moselle wine. At midday Hegel travelled alone to Elberfeld, crossing the Wupper again, among students smoking pipes.
